title: Transition metals
unit: A2 Unit 4 (inferred from content; confirm against the paper cover)

questions.question: Identify the salt bridge solution and the electrode and solution needed in the right-hand half-cell to measure the standard electrode potential of Fe3+/Fe2+ under standard conditions.
questions.answer: A: potassium nitrate solution (KNO3(aq)); B: platinum (Pt); C: a solution containing both Fe3+(aq) and Fe2+(aq), each at 1.0 mol dm-3
steps: A salt bridge needs a solution of unreactive ions, such as KNO3(aq), so it completes the circuit without reacting with either half-cell.
B is an inert electrode, platinum, because Fe3+/Fe2+ has no solid metal to act as the electrode and Pt carries electrons to the solution.
C must contain both members of the redox couple, Fe3+(aq) and Fe2+(aq).
Standard conditions: each ion at 1.0 mol dm-3, 298 K (and 100 kPa for the hydrogen half-cell).

questions.question: Given a cell diagram, write the two half-equations and the overall ionic equation (no state symbols).
questions.answer: Left (oxidation): Mn2+ + 4H2O -> MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e-; right (reduction): BiO3- + 6H+ + 2e- -> Bi3+ + 3H2O; overall: 2Mn2+ + 5BiO3- + 14H+ -> 2MnO4- + 5Bi3+ + 7H2O
steps: In a cell diagram the left-hand electrode is where oxidation occurs: Mn2+ + 4H2O -> MnO4- + 8H+ + 5e-.
The right-hand electrode is where reduction occurs: BiO3- + 6H+ + 2e- -> Bi3+ + 3H2O.
Balance the electrons: multiply the Mn half-equation by 2 and the Bi half-equation by 5, so 10e- cancel.
Cancel H2O and H+ to give 2Mn2+ + 5BiO3- + 14H+ -> 2MnO4- + 5Bi3+ + 7H2O (charge 13+ on each side).

questions.question: E-zero for Cr3+/Cr is -0.74 V. Calculate the electrode potential at 298 K when [Cr3+] = 0.0100 mol dm-3.
steps: Half-equation: Cr3+ + 3e- -> Cr, so n = 3.
Nernst equation: E = E-zero + (RT/nF) ln[Cr3+].

questions.question: How many isomers containing a benzene ring have molecular formula C6H3(NO2)2OH? Options: A 4, B 5, C 6, D 7.
steps: The benzene ring carries three substituents: one OH and two NO2.
Count the distinct arrangements of 1 OH and 2 NO2 on a benzene ring.
The six distinct positional isomers are 2,3-; 2,4-; 2,5-; 2,6-; 3,4-; 3,5-dinitrophenol.
So the answer is C, 6.

questions.question: 22.0 cm3 of MnO4- oxidises 25.0 cm3 of Fe2+ in acid (MnO4- -> Mn2+). What volume of the same MnO4- is needed to oxidise the same Fe2+ in neutral conditions (MnO4- -> MnO2)? Options: A 12.6, B 13.2, C 36.7, D 38.5 cm3.
steps: Acid: Mn goes from +7 to +2, so 5 electrons per MnO4-.
Neutral: Mn goes from +7 to +4, so 3 electrons per MnO4-.
The same moles of Fe2+ are oxidised, so the moles of MnO4- scale inversely with electrons gained.
Neutral volume = 22.0 x (5/3) = 36.7 cm3.

questions.question: Phenol reacts 1:1 with ethanoyl chloride to give phenyl ethanoate. 3.67 g of product formed with 85.0% yield. What was the starting mass of phenol? Options: A 2.16 g, B 2.54 g, C 2.98 g, D 4.51 g.
steps: Mr of phenyl ethanoate (C8H8O2) = 136; Mr of phenol (C6H5OH) = 94.
Moles of product actually formed = 3.67 / 136 = 0.0270 mol.
Theoretical moles = 0.0270 / 0.850 = 0.0317 mol (1:1 with phenol).
Mass of phenol = 0.0317 x 94 = 2.98 g.

questions.question: A hydrocarbon contains 91.3% carbon by mass. Which could be its molecular formula? Options: A C6H6, B C7H8, C C8H10, D C9H12.
questions.answer: B - C7H8
steps: Percentage C = (mass C / Mr) x 100 for each option.
C7H8: 84/92 = 91.3%, which matches.
So the answer is B.

questions.question: 25.0 cm3 of a methane and ethane mixture needs 65.0 cm3 O2 for complete combustion, all at the same T and p. Find the percentage by volume of methane.
questions.answer: 60% methane by volume
steps: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O, so 2 volumes O2 per volume CH4.
C2H6 + 3.5O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O, so 3.5 volumes O2 per volume C2H6.
Let x = CH4 and y = C2H6: x + y = 25.0 and 2x + 3.5y = 65.0.
Solve: y = 10.0 and x = 15.0 cm3.

questions.question: Devise a three-step reaction scheme converting butan-2-ol into 1-amino-2-methylbutan-2-ol, giving reagents, conditions and equations. Use [O] and [H] for oxidation and reduction.
questions.answer: Butan-2-ol -[O]-> butanone -HCN (KCN then dilute acid)-> 2-hydroxy-2-methylbutanenitrile -[H] (LiAlH4, dry ether)-> 1-amino-2-methylbutan-2-ol
steps: Step 1: oxidise with [O] (acidified K2Cr2O7, heat, distil off the ketone): CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 -> CH3COCH2CH3.
Step 2: add HCN across the C=O (NaCN or KCN, then dilute acid, room temperature): gives CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CN.
The nucleophilic addition of CN- adds one carbon, which is why the product has five carbons.
Step 3: reduce the nitrile with [H] (LiAlH4 in dry ether, then water) to CH2NH2.
Equation: CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CN + 4[H] -> CH3CH2C(OH)(CH3)CH2NH2.

questions.question: What is an organic product of ethylamine reacting with chloroethane? Options: A NH2CH2COCl, B C2H5NH Cl-, C C2H5NHCOC2H5, D (C2H5)2NH Cl-.
questions.answer: D - (C2H5)2NH2+ Cl- (diethylammonium chloride)
steps: Ethylamine acts as a nucleophile and attacks the C-Cl carbon of chloroethane.
This gives a secondary ammonium salt: (C2H5)2NH2+ Cl-.
Option B has the wrong number of ethyl groups; option C is an amide, not formed here.
So the answer is D.

questions.question: Which pair of monomers can form the polymer shown?
questions.answer: D: HOOCC6H4COOH and HOCH2CH2OH
steps: The repeat unit contains ester links (-C(=O)-O-), so the polymer is a polyester made by condensation polymerisation.
The acyl part is -OC-C6H4-CO-, which comes from benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid, HOOCC6H4COOH.
The alkoxy part is -O-CH2CH2-O-, which comes from ethane-1,2-diol, HOCH2CH2OH.
So the monomer pair is a dicarboxylic acid plus a diol, option D.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electronic structure, why iron(III) compounds are more stable than iron(II) compounds.
questions.answer: Fe3+ is 3d5 (half-filled d subshell, extra stability); Fe2+ is 3d6.
steps: Fe2+ is [Ar] 3d6; Fe3+ is [Ar] 3d5.
A half-filled d subshell (3d5) has extra stability from exchange energy and symmetry.
So Fe3+ is more stable than Fe2+.

questions.question: Write the equation for the third ionisation energy of iron, including state symbols.
steps: The third ionisation energy removes the third electron from a gaseous ion.
Start from the 2+ ion, which is Fe2+(g).
Products are Fe3+(g) and one electron.

questions.question: Explain how stable Fe3+ ions can form from Fe2+ ions in aqueous solution, referring only to the relevant energy changes. The third ionisation energy of iron is 2958 kJ mol-1.
questions.answer: The large third ionisation energy is offset by the much more exothermic hydration enthalpy of Fe3+.
steps: Forming Fe3+(g) from Fe2+(g) needs the third ionisation energy, +2958 kJ mol-1 (endothermic).
Fe3+ is smaller and has a higher charge than Fe2+, so it has a higher charge density.
The hydration enthalpy of Fe3+(aq) is much more exothermic than that of Fe2+(aq).
This larger release of hydration energy makes the overall change exothermic and so feasible in solution.

questions.question: Explain why oxyhaemocyanin (copper complex) and oxyhaemoglobin (iron complex) have different colours.
questions.answer: Different metal ions and ligand environments give different d-orbital energy gaps, so different wavelengths of visible light are absorbed.
steps: Each complex has a central metal ion with a partly filled d subshell that is split by the ligands.
The size of the energy gap between split d levels depends on the metal ion and the ligands.
The copper and iron complexes have different gaps.
They absorb different visible wavelengths, so they transmit different complementary colours.

questions.question: Using the calibration graph, decide whether the iron content of 20 g sodium carbonate (transmittance 39.8%, 500 cm3 solution) meets a limit of less than 20 ppm.
questions.answer: Iron = about 11 ppm by mass (0.45 mg dm-3 from the graph), which is less than 20 ppm, so the sample meets the specification.
steps: log(% transmittance) = log 39.8 = 1.60.
Reading across the calibration graph from 1.60 to the line gives a concentration of about 0.45 mg dm-3 of iron.
Mass of iron in 500 cm3 = 0.45 mg dm-3 x 0.500 dm3 = 0.225 mg = 2.25 x 10^-4 g.
ppm by mass = (2.25 x 10^-4 g / 20 g) x 10^6 = 11 ppm.
11 ppm < 20 ppm, so the sodium carbonate meets the stated specification.

questions.question: Suggest what type of ligand thioglycolic acid is in the iron(III) complex, and justify your answer.
questions.answer: Bidentate: it donates through two atoms (S and O), forming two dative bonds.
steps: Thioglycolic acid, HSCH2COOH, has a sulfur atom with lone pairs and a carboxyl oxygen with lone pairs.
Each of these donor atoms can donate a lone pair to Fe3+, forming a dative covalent bond.
Two donor atoms per ligand means it is bidentate (forms a chelate ring).

questions.question: State why the iron(II) catalyst is described as homogeneous.
questions.answer: It is in the same physical state (aqueous solution) as the reactant ions.
steps: Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as the reactants.
Fe2+ and the I- and S2O8 2- ions are all aqueous, so the catalyst is in the same phase.

questions.question: Write two equations showing how Fe2+ ions catalyse the oxidation of iodide ions by peroxodisulfate ions (no state symbols).
steps: Step 1: Fe2+ is oxidised by peroxodisulfate: 2Fe2+ + S2O8 2- -> 2Fe3+ + 2SO4 2-.
Step 2: Fe3+ oxidises iodide and is reduced back: 2Fe3+ + 2I- -> 2Fe2+ + I2.
Check: adding gives the overall equation with Fe2+ unchanged.

questions.question: Suggest how Fe2+ ions lower the activation energy of the iodide and peroxodisulfate reaction.
questions.answer: They provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy via Fe3+ intermediates.
steps: Fe2+ reacts with S2O8 2- and then the Fe3+ reacts with I-.
Each step has a lower activation energy than the direct uncatalysed collision.
So more collisions have enough energy to react.

questions.question: Give a possible reason why the chloro complexes of iron ions have a coordination number of four rather than six.
questions.answer: Chloride ligands are larger than water, so only four can fit around the iron ion.
steps: Chloride ions are much larger than water molecules.
Steric crowding limits how many chloride ligands can fit around the central Fe ion.
So four chloride ligands form a tetrahedral complex, [FeCl4]-.

questions.question: Aqueous NaOH is added to aqueous iron(II) sulfate and the mixture allowed to stand. What would be observed? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: D: green precipitate immediately, which turns brown on standing
steps: Fe2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) -> Fe(OH)2(s), which is a green precipitate.
On standing in air the Fe(OH)2 is oxidised by oxygen to Fe(OH)3, which is brown.
So the observations are green precipitate then turns brown, option D.

questions.question: Deduce the formulae of the ions responsible for the colours of orange solution F and green solution G.
questions.answer: F: Cr2O7 2- (orange); G: Cr3+ (green, as [Cr(H2O)6]3+)
steps: Orange acidified solution F contains dichromate ions, Cr2O7 2-.
Warming with ethanol reduces dichromate, Cr(VI) to Cr(III).
Green solution G contains Cr3+ ions (hexaaqua complex in water).

questions.question: Write the overall equation for the reaction in the cell (F with ethanol to give ethanal and G), no state symbols.
questions.answer: 3C2H5OH + Cr2O7 2- + 8H+ -> 3CH3CHO + 2Cr3+ + 7H2O
steps: Ethanol to ethanal loses 2 electrons per molecule: 3 molecules give 6 e-.
Dichromate, Cr(VI) to Cr(III), gains 3 e- per Cr, so 2 Cr gain 6 e-.
Balance H+ and water: 8H+ on left, 7H2O on right.
Check atoms and charge: left +6, right 2(+3) = +6.

questions.question: E is a yellow crystalline solid that dissolves to a yellow solution, and dilute sulfuric acid turns it orange. Write the ionic equation for E with dilute sulfuric acid (no state symbols).
steps: E is a chromate(VI) salt (yellow CrO4 2- ions).
Acid converts chromate to dichromate, which is orange.
Balance: 2CrO4 2- + 2H+ -> Cr2O7 2- + H2O.

questions.question: State the property of transition metals such as titanium that makes their compounds effective catalysts.
questions.answer: Variable oxidation states (they can change oxidation state).
steps: Transition metal ions can be oxidised and reduced by changing oxidation state.
This lets them take part in redox steps and form intermediates in catalysis.

questions.question: State the meaning of the terms monodentate and ligand.
questions.answer: A ligand is a species that donates a lone pair to a central metal ion; monodentate means it forms one dative bond.
steps: A ligand is an electron-pair donor (lone pair) that forms a dative covalent bond to a metal ion.
Monodentate means the ligand has one donor atom so it forms one bond to the central metal.

questions.question: Complex Z is a stereoisomer of complex Y. Complete the diagram showing the arrangement of the ligands in Z.
questions.answer: Z is the facial (fac) isomer: draw Cl at the top and at the end of the right-hand dotted bond, and THF at the end of the right-hand wedge, so the 3 Cl are mutually cis and the 3 THF are mutually cis.
steps: Complex Y is octahedral TiCl3(THF)3 in which two THF are trans (top and bottom) and two Cl are trans (right-hand dotted bond and left-hand wedge), so Y is the meridional (mer) isomer.
The stereoisomer Z must have the same ligands but a different arrangement, which is the facial (fac) isomer with all three like ligands on one triangular face.
The given ligands in Z are THF at the bottom, THF on the left wedge and Cl on the left dotted bond.
Complete Z with THF on the right wedge (cis to both THF already shown), and Cl on the top vertical bond and the right dotted bond, so no two like ligands are trans to each other.

questions.question: State the colour change observed at the end-point of the Ti3+ titration with alizarin indicator.
questions.answer: From green to yellow
steps: Alizarin is green in the presence of Ti3+ and yellow in the presence of TiO2+.
At the end-point all Ti3+ has been oxidised, so the colour changes from green to yellow.

questions.question: Mg(NO3)2.6H2O (0.750 g in 100.0 cm3). 10.0 cm3 titrated with 0.0850 mol dm-3 Ti3+, end-point at 20.70 cm3. Mr = 256.3. Find the final oxidation state of nitrogen.
questions.answer: +2 (nitrogen reduced from +5 to +2, i.e. NO)
steps: In the 10.0 cm3 aliquot: 2.926 x 10^-4 mol, giving 2 x 2.926 x 10^-4 = 5.85 x 10^-4 mol NO3-.
Moles Ti3+ oxidised = 0.0850 x 0.02070 = 1.760 x 10^-3 mol, so electrons transferred = 1.760 x 10^-3 mol.
Nitrogen gains 3 electrons, so it goes from +5 to +2.

questions.question: Write the overall ionic equation for the titration using the answer to (c)(ii) and the half-equations from the list below.
questions.answer: 3Ti3+ + NO3- + H2O -> 3TiO2+ + NO + 2H+
steps: From (c)(ii) nitrogen is reduced from +5 to +2, so the relevant half-equation is NO3- + 4H+ + 3e- -> NO + 2H2O.
Ti3+ is oxidised: Ti3+ + H2O -> TiO2+ + 2H+ + e-, so multiply by 3 to match the 3 electrons.
Add: 3Ti3+ + 3H2O + NO3- + 4H+ -> 3TiO2+ + 6H+ + NO + 2H2O.
Cancel H2O and H+ to give 3Ti3+ + NO3- + H2O -> 3TiO2+ + NO + 2H+ (charge 8+ on both sides).

questions.question: Use the electrode potential data provided to calculate E-zero for the overall titration reaction.
questions.answer: E-zero(cell) = +0.86 V
steps: The NO3-/NO half-equation (+0.96 V) is reduction and the TiO2+/Ti3+ half-equation (+0.10 V) is reversed to oxidation.
E-zero(cell) = E-zero(reduction) - E-zero(oxidation) = (+0.96) - (+0.10) = +0.86 V.

questions.question: Suggest why the contents of the conical flask are heated during the titration.
questions.answer: To increase the rate of reaction so the titration proceeds at a reasonable speed.
steps: The reaction between Ti3+ and nitrate is slow at room temperature.
Heating increases the kinetic energy and collision rate, speeding the reaction up.

questions.question: Assess the teacher's claim that the titration can be done without alizarin because TiCl3 is blue and TiO2+ is colourless. Name a coloured complex ion in water, explain its colour, and suggest why alizarin gives more accurate results.
questions.answer: Partly valid: [Ti(H2O)6]3+ is coloured by d-d transitions, but the colour change is less distinct than alizarin's green-to-yellow change, so alizarin improves accuracy.
steps: A coloured complex present when TiCl3 dissolves is the hexaaqua ion [Ti(H2O)6]3+.
Ti3+ has one d electron, which is split into two levels by the water ligands.
It absorbs light to promote the electron (d-d transition), and the colour seen is the complementary colour.
The teacher is partly right: the solution is coloured, so the endpoint from coloured to colourless is harder to judge.
Alizarin gives a sharp green-to-yellow colour change, which is easier to see and so more accurate.
Conclusion: the statement is incomplete; an indicator is still useful.

questions.question: What type of ligand is 1,2-diaminoethane and what is the coordination number of copper(II) in Cu(en)3 2+? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: B: bidentate, coordination number 6
steps: 1,2-diaminoethane, H2NCH2CH2NH2, has two N atoms, each donating a lone pair, so it is bidentate.
Cu(en)3 2+ has three bidentate ligands, so the coordination number is 3 x 2 = 6.

questions.question: Aqueous ammonia added to zinc sulfate forms a white precipitate that dissolves in excess. What types of reaction occur? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: A: deprotonation then ligand exchange
steps: NH3 first acts as a base and removes H+ from [Zn(H2O)6]2+, giving neutral Zn(OH)2(H2O)4, the white precipitate (deprotonation).
In excess ammonia, NH3 replaces water ligands to give colourless [Zn(NH3)4]2+, so this step is ligand exchange.
So the pair is deprotonation, ligand exchange, option A.

questions.question: Which atom has the greatest number of unpaired electrons? Options: A chromium, B iron, C manganese, D vanadium.
questions.answer: A - chromium (6 unpaired electrons)
steps: Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1: 6 unpaired electrons.
Fe is [Ar] 3d6 4s2: 4 unpaired electrons.
Mn is [Ar] 3d5 4s2: 5 unpaired electrons.
V is [Ar] 3d3 4s2: 3 unpaired electrons.
So chromium has the most.

questions.question: The reaction of ethanedioate ions with manganate(VII) ions in acid involves autocatalysis. What is the catalyst? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: C: Mn2+
steps: The reaction is autocatalytic, so the catalyst is one of the products.
Mn2+ is formed in the reaction and then catalyses it (via Mn3+), so the rate increases once some has formed.
The other products, H2O and CO2, are not catalysts; MnO4- and H+ are reactants, so the answer is Mn2+.

questions.question: Which statement best explains carbon monoxide poisoning? Options: A CO binds irreversibly to haemoglobin, B CO forms stronger dative bonds with haemoglobin than O2, C carboxyhaemoglobin formation gives a large entropy increase, D CO has a triple bond whereas O2 has a double bond.
questions.answer: B - CO forms stronger dative covalent bonds with haemoglobin than oxygen does
steps: CO binds to the Fe2+ in haem by dative covalent bonding.
The bond is much stronger than the O2 bond, so O2 cannot bind.
Option A is wrong because the binding is strong but not irreversible.
Options C and D do not explain the poisoning.

questions.question: Iodide ions are oxidised by peroxodisulfate ions in aqueous solution (2I- + S2O8 2- -> I2 + 2SO4 2-). The reaction is catalysed by adding Fe2+ ions. This catalysis is effective because: A Fe2+ reacts with iodide ions and with peroxodisulfate ions, B Fe2+ has many electrons in its outermost subshells, C Fe2+ has many active sites on which the reaction can occur, D Fe2+ is readily oxidised to Fe3+ which is then reduced to Fe2+.
questions.answer: D - Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+, which is then reduced back to Fe2+
steps: The catalyst is regenerated at the end of the reaction.
Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ by peroxodisulfate and Fe3+ is reduced back by iodide.
This redox cycle is why Fe2+ is effective, so option D is correct.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the mechanism of platinum as a catalyst in car exhaust treatment with that of vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact Process (general catalyst definitions not required).
questions.answer: Both are heterogeneous. Pt adsorbs gases on its surface without changing its oxidation state; V2O5 is reduced and reoxidised, so V changes oxidation state.
steps: Both are solid catalysts, so both are heterogeneous and provide a surface.
Pt: CO and NO are adsorbed onto the surface, weakening bonds; adjacent molecules react and products desorb.
Pt keeps its oxidation state, unchanged, during the reaction.
V2O5: SO2 reduces V(V) to V(IV), e.g. SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + 2VO2.
V(IV) is reoxidised by O2: 2VO2 + 1/2 O2 -> V2O5, so V cycles between +4 and +5.
Contrast: the Pt mechanism uses surface adsorption; the V2O5 mechanism uses a redox cycle with the solid oxide.

questions.question: Iodide ions are oxidised by peroxodisulfate. Which statement is true? A both Fe2+ and Fe3+ catalyse, B only Fe2+, C only Fe3+, D neither.
questions.answer: A - both Fe2+ and Fe3+ catalyse the reaction
steps: Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ by peroxodisulfate: this step uses Fe2+.
Fe3+ oxidises iodide and is reduced back to Fe2+: this step uses Fe3+.
Both ions are part of the catalytic cycle, so both catalyse the reaction.

questions.question: Which is not true of the reactions in a catalytic converter? A heterogeneous catalysis, B CO adsorbed onto the catalyst surface, C N2 desorbed from the surface, D the products cause no harm to the environment.
questions.answer: D - the products cause no harm to the environment (CO2 is a greenhouse gas)
steps: Heterogeneous catalysis is correct: the catalyst is a solid surface.
CO is adsorbed on the surface and N2 is desorbed, so options B and C are true.
The product CO2 is a greenhouse gas, so option D is false.

questions.question: Cobalt chloride is used as a test for water. This depends on: A anhydrous CoCl2 is blue and hydrated CoCl2 is pink, B anhydrous pink and hydrated blue, C CoCl2 blue and CoCl3 pink, D CoCl2 pink and CoCl3 blue.
questions.answer: A - anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and hydrated cobalt(II) chloride is pink
steps: Anhydrous CoCl2 is blue.
Hydrated CoCl2 (as [Co(H2O)6]2+) is pink.
Adding water turns blue to pink, which is the test.

questions.question: What are the shapes of the Pt(NH3)2Cl2 complex and the chromium complex? (Chromium complex formula shown in the figure below.)
questions.answer: D: Pt(NH3)2Cl2 is square planar and CrCl4- is tetrahedral
steps: Pt(II) forms four-coordinate complexes that are square planar, as in cisplatin.
CrCl4- has four large Cl- ligands around Cr, so it is tetrahedral (large ligands favour tetrahedral four-coordination).
This is option D.

questions.question: What is the bonding between the ligands and the central atom in these complexes? (Chromium complex formula missing.)
questions.answer: B: the bonding in both complexes is dative covalent
steps: In a complex each ligand (NH3, Cl-) donates a lone pair to the central metal ion.
So the bond between ligand and central atom is a dative (coordinate) covalent bond in both Pt(NH3)2Cl2 and CrCl4-.

keywords: species P Q R S T V W
questions.question: Identify, by name or formula, the copper-containing species P, Q, R, S, T, V and W in the reaction sequence diagram.
questions.answer: P = copper (Cu, copper metal); Q = copper(II) sulfate solution (Cu2+(aq)); R = copper(II) hydroxide (Cu(OH)2); S = copper(II) oxide (CuO); T = tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ion, [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+; V = diamminecopper(I) ion, [Cu(NH3)2]+; W = copper(II) nitrate solution (Cu2+(aq), [Cu(H2O)6]2+)
steps: Copper(I) iodide disproportionates in H2SO4: 2Cu+ -> Cu + Cu2+, so P (pink solid) is Cu metal and Q (blue solution) is Cu2+ as CuSO4(aq).
A little NH3(aq) added to Cu2+(aq) gives the pale blue precipitate R = Cu(OH)2 (copper(II) hydroxide).
Heating Cu(OH)2 gives black S = CuO (copper(II) oxide).
Excess NH3 dissolves R by ligand exchange to give the dark blue complex T = [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+.
CuI + NH3 gives the colourless complex V = [Cu(NH3)2]+ (copper(I) complex).
CuO + HNO3 gives blue W = Cu(NO3)2(aq), i.e. [Cu(H2O)6]2+ (copper(II) nitrate).

questions.question: Name the type of chemical species that T and V are. (Diagram needed.)
questions.answer: Complex ions (T is a copper(II) ammine complex and V is a copper(I) ammine complex)
steps: T is [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ and V is [Cu(NH3)2]+.
Both are complex ions: a central metal ion surrounded by ligands bonded by dative covalent bonds.

questions.question: Explain why T is coloured while V is colourless. (Diagram needed to identify T and V.)
questions.answer: T contains Cu2+ (3d9), which has a partially filled d subshell, so d-d transitions can absorb visible light; V contains Cu+ (3d10) with a full d subshell, so no d-d transitions and it is colourless.
steps: Colour in transition metal complexes arises from d-d transitions: an electron is promoted between split d orbitals by absorbing visible light.
In T the copper is Cu2+ with the configuration [Ar] 3d9, so there is a vacancy in the d orbitals and an electron can be promoted.
In V the copper is Cu+ with the configuration [Ar] 3d10, so the d subshell is full and there is no empty d orbital to be promoted into.
With no d-d transition no visible light is absorbed, so V is colourless.

questions.question: Suggest an explanation for the change of V into T on shaking. (Diagram needed.)
questions.answer: Vigorous shaking mixes in oxygen from the air, which oxidises copper(I) in V to copper(II), forming the dark blue complex T.
steps: V contains [Cu(NH3)2]+, in which copper is in the +1 oxidation state.
Shaking dissolves oxygen from the air, and O2 oxidises Cu+ to Cu2+.
The Cu2+ then forms the dark blue complex [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ with the excess ammonia, which is T.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation for the disproportionation of copper(I) in sulfuric acid (no state symbols).
questions.answer: 2Cu+ -> Cu2+ + Cu
steps: Copper(I) is both oxidised (to Cu2+) and reduced (to Cu metal).
Balance: 2Cu+ -> Cu2+ + Cu.

questions.question: Show that the disproportionation in (c)(i) is thermodynamically feasible using standard electrode potentials from the Data Booklet.
questions.answer: E-zero(cell) = +0.37 V, which is positive, so the disproportionation is feasible.
steps: From the Data Booklet: Cu+ + e- <=> Cu has E-zero = +0.52 V, and Cu2+ + e- <=> Cu+ has E-zero = +0.15 V.
In 2Cu+ -> Cu2+ + Cu one Cu+ is reduced (+0.52 V) and another is oxidised (the Cu2+/Cu+ half-cell, +0.15 V).
E-zero(cell) = E-zero(reduction) - E-zero(oxidation) = (+0.52) - (+0.15) = +0.37 V.
A positive E-zero(cell) means the reaction is thermodynamically feasible.

questions.question: Calculate n, the moles of water of crystallisation in mitscherlichite, from a 4.26 g sample titrated by iodometry (mean titre 26.65 cm3 of 0.0500 mol dm-3 thiosulfate).
questions.answer: n = 2 (mitscherlichite is K2CuCl4.2H2O, Mr about 320)
steps: Moles of thiosulfate = 0.0500 x 0.02665 = 1.3325 x 10^-3 mol.
From the equations, 2 S2O3 2- reacts with 1 I2, and 2 Cu2+ forms 1 I2, so mol Cu2+ = mol S2O3 2- = 1.3325 x 10^-3 mol in the 25.0 cm3 portion.
In the whole 250.0 cm3: 1.3325 x 10^-2 mol Cu2+, which is the moles of mitscherlichite.

questions.question: Diamminecopper(I) ions are not coloured because: A d orbitals cannot be split, B the energy gap is outside the visible range, C d-d transitions are not possible because the d orbitals are full, D copper(I) is readily oxidised.
questions.answer: C - d-d transitions are not possible because the d orbitals are fully occupied
steps: Copper(I) is 3d10, so all d orbitals are full.
No electron can be promoted between split d levels, so no d-d absorption occurs.
So the complex is colourless.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of a chromium atom? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: A: [Ar] 3d5 4s1
steps: Chromium is an exception: one 4s electron moves into the 3d subshell to give a half-filled 3d subshell.
Configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s1 has five unpaired electrons in 3d and one in 4s, option A.

questions.question: On formation from [Ni(H2O)6]2+, which complex gives the most positive increase in entropy of the system? Options: A [NiCl4]2-, B [Ni(EDTA)]2-, C [Ni(C2O4)2]2-, D [Ni(H2NCH2CH2NH2)3]2+.
questions.answer: D - [Ni(H2NCH2CH2NH2)3]2+
steps: Entropy increases when the number of particles in the system increases.
Option D: [Ni(H2O)6]2+ + 3 en gives [Ni(en)3]2+ + 6 H2O, so 4 particles become 7.
Three bidentate en ligands release six water molecules, the largest increase in particle number.
So D gives the most positive entropy change.

questions.question: A ligand must be an: A electron-pair donor, B electron-pair donor and negatively charged, C electron-pair acceptor, D electron-pair acceptor and negatively charged.
questions.answer: A - electron-pair donor
steps: A ligand donates a lone pair to a metal ion.
It does not need to be negatively charged (e.g. NH3 and H2O are neutral).
So the answer is A.

questions.question: Nickel is classified as a transition metal because: A it is a d-block element, B it has partially filled d orbitals, C it forms stable ions with partially filled d orbitals, D it forms stable compounds with different oxidation states.
questions.answer: C - it forms stable ions with partially filled d orbitals
steps: Transition element definition: an element that forms one or more stable ions with a partially filled d subshell.
Option A only describes its position in the periodic table.
Option C matches the definition, as Ni2+ is 3d8.

questions.question: Aqueous ammonia is added drop by drop to a solution of cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl2(aq), until in excess. What would be the sequence of observations? A blue solution -> pink precipitate -> dark blue solution, B pink solution -> blue precipitate, C blue solution -> pink precipitate, D pink solution -> blue precipitate -> yellow-brown solution.
questions.answer: D - pink solution, blue precipitate, yellow-brown solution
steps: [Co(H2O)6]2+ is pink in solution.
Small amounts of ammonia precipitate blue Co(OH)2.
Excess ammonia forms [Co(NH3)6]2+, which is oxidised by air to a yellow-brown solution.
So the sequence is option D.

questions.question: Which ion is most likely to catalyse the reaction between peroxodisulfate and I-? Options: A Cl-, B Fe2+, C Cu2+, D Cu+. (E-zero table in diagram.)
questions.answer: B: Fe2+
steps: A catalyst for S2O8 2- + 2I- needs a redox couple with E-zero between +0.54 V (I2/I-) and +2.01 V (S2O8 2-/SO4 2-).
Fe3+/Fe2+ (+0.77 V) lies between them: Fe2+ is oxidised by S2O8 2- and the Fe3+ formed oxidises I- back to Fe2+.
Cl-/Cl2 (+1.36 V) lies between them but it is oxidised by S2O8 2-, so it is not regenerated; Cu2+/Cu+ (+0.15 V) is below +0.54 V, so Cu2+ cannot oxidise I-.
So the best catalyst is Fe2+ (option B).

questions.question: (Part (a) concerns the catalysed reaction S2O8 2- + 2I- -> 2SO4 2- + I2.) Which term best describes the type of catalyst for the reaction in part (a)? A autocatalyst, B biocatalyst, C heterogeneous, D homogeneous.
questions.answer: D - homogeneous
steps: Iron(II) is an aqueous ion and the reactants are aqueous, so they are in the same phase.
That makes it a homogeneous catalyst.

questions.question: Which substance is manufactured in a process involving a reaction catalysed by vanadium(V) oxide? A ammonia, B nitric acid, C sodium hydroxide, D sulfuric acid.
questions.answer: D - sulfuric acid
steps: V2O5 catalyses the oxidation of SO2 to SO3 in the Contact Process.
SO3 is absorbed to make sulfuric acid.

questions.question: What is the electronic configuration of the Fe2+ ion? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: B: [Ar] 3d6 (3d: one pair of electrons and four unpaired, 4s empty)
steps: Fe is [Ar] 3d6 4s2; transition metals lose the 4s electrons first to form ions.
Fe2+ is therefore [Ar] 3d6 4s0, with 4s empty.
Six 3d electrons fill the orbitals by Hund's rule: one orbital holds a pair and the other four hold single electrons, which is option B.

questions.question: 2.72 g of brass dissolved in nitric acid; Cu2+ reduced to Cu+ and precipitated as 4.69 g CuSCN. Calculate the percentage of copper and determine whether this is a gilding metal.
questions.answer: Copper = 90.0% by mass. This is within the 89% to 95% range (5% to 11% zinc), so it is a gilding metal.
steps: Moles CuSCN = 4.69 / 121.6 = 0.0386 mol; each CuSCN comes from one Cu2+ (via Cu+), so moles Cu = 0.0386 mol.
Mass of copper = 0.0386 x 63.5 = 2.45 g.
Percentage Cu = 2.45 / 2.72 x 100 = 90.0%, so zinc is about 10.0%.
Gilding metal contains 5% to 11% zinc, so 10.0% zinc is in range and the brass is a gilding metal.

questions.question: Explain, using thermodynamic and kinetic factors, why sulfite reduces Cu2+ to Cu+ but does not reduce Cu+ to Cu.
questions.answer: Thermodynamics: Cu2+ to Cu+ has E-zero(cell) of about -0.02 V (close to zero, so feasible under real conditions), while Cu+ to Cu has +0.35 V (feasible), so thermodynamics alone allows both. Kinetics: the reduction of Cu+ to Cu must have a high activation energy, so it is too slow to occur.
steps: HSO3- is the reductant, so the HSO4-/HSO3- half-cell (+0.17 V) is reversed to oxidation.
Cu2+ to Cu+: E-zero(cell) = 0.15 - 0.17 = -0.02 V, which is almost zero, so the reaction is only marginally unfavourable and goes with non-standard concentrations (excess reductant).
Cu+ to Cu: E-zero(cell) = 0.52 - 0.17 = +0.35 V, which is positive, so this reduction is thermodynamically feasible.
It does not happen, so it is kinetically hindered: the reaction has a high activation energy and is too slow at the conditions used.

questions.question: A student suggests precipitating Zn2+ with a large excess of NaOH. Comment by describing the reactions as excess NaOH is added.
questions.answer: Zn2+ forms a white Zn(OH)2 precipitate, which redissolves in excess NaOH to form [Zn(OH)4]2-, so the suggestion is poor.
steps: Zn2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) -> Zn(OH)2(s): a white precipitate forms.
Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric, so it dissolves in excess NaOH.
Zn(OH)2(s) + 2OH-(aq) -> [Zn(OH)4]2-(aq): a colourless solution forms.
So adding excess NaOH does not remove all Zn2+, and the suggestion is not valid.

questions.question: Suggest why gilding metals are less malleable than pure copper, considering their structure.
questions.answer: Zinc atoms of different size distort the regular layers of copper atoms, so the layers cannot slide easily.
steps: Pure copper has a regular lattice of layers that slide over each other.
Zn atoms are a different size, which distorts the regular layers.
The layers cannot slide easily, so the alloy is less malleable.

questions.question: Draw a labelled diagram of the apparatus to measure the emf of a Cu/Zn cell under standard conditions.
questions.answer: Two half-cells joined by a salt bridge and a high-resistance voltmeter: a copper electrode in 1.00 mol dm-3 Cu2+(aq) and a zinc electrode in 1.00 mol dm-3 Zn2+(aq), at 298 K.
steps: Left beaker: zinc metal strip dipping into 1.00 mol dm-3 ZnSO4(aq), labelled with the solution and electrode.
Right beaker: copper metal strip dipping into 1.00 mol dm-3 CuSO4(aq).
Salt bridge (filter paper or tube soaked in saturated KNO3(aq)) dipping into both solutions.
High-resistance voltmeter connected by wires between the two metal electrodes; temperature 298 K.

questions.question: A cell has Cu2+ at 1.00 mol dm-3 and Zn2+ at unknown concentration, emf +1.09 V. Calculate the zinc ion concentration (use the Data Booklet page 10).
questions.answer: [Zn2+] = 2.2 mol dm-3
steps: Data Booklet: Cu2+/Cu E-zero = +0.34 V and Zn2+/Zn E-zero = -0.76 V, so E-zero(cell) = 0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V.
Cu2+ is at 1.00 mol dm-3, so the copper half-cell stays at +0.34 V; Nernst for zinc: E(Zn) = -0.76 + (0.0260/2) ln[Zn2+].

questions.question: How many of the four ions shown contain a metal with oxidation number +3? (Formulae shown as a diagram.)
questions.answer: B: two
steps: [CrCl2(H2O)4]+: Cr = +3 (2 x -1 = -2, water is neutral, so Cr = +1 + 2 = +3).
Two ions (AlO2- and [CrCl2(H2O)4]+) contain a +3 metal, option B.

questions.question: When oxygen binds to the haem group in haemoglobin, each oxygen molecule: A bonds reversibly to an iron(II) ion, B bonds irreversibly, C replaces an iron(II) ion reversibly, D replaces an iron(II) ion irreversibly.
questions.answer: A - bonds reversibly to an iron(II) ion
steps: O2 binds to Fe2+ in the haem group by a dative bond.
The binding is reversible so O2 can be released in tissues.
Fe2+ is not replaced, so C and D are wrong.

questions.question: Viridian (a blue-green pigment, formula not in text) loses 19.15% of its mass on heating to drive off water. Identify element M.
questions.answer: M = Cr (chromium); viridian is Cr2O3.2H2O
steps: Mass lost on heating is the water of crystallisation: 2H2O = 2 x 18.0 = 36.0 per formula unit.
This is 19.15% of the total Mr, so Mr(M2O3.2H2O) = 36.0 / 0.1915 = 188.0.
Ar(M) = 52.0, which is chromium (Cr).

questions.question: Name the type of reaction occurring when concentrated hydrochloric acid is added to aqueous cobalt(II) sulfate.
questions.answer: Ligand substitution (ligand exchange)
steps: Chloride ions replace water ligands in the complex ion.
This is a ligand substitution reaction.

questions.question: Write an ionic equation for the reaction when concentrated HCl is added to aqueous cobalt(II) sulfate (no state symbols).
steps: Pink [Co(H2O)6]2+ reacts with Cl- ions.
Four Cl- replace six water ligands, giving blue [CoCl4]2-.
Balance: [Co(H2O)6]2+ + 4Cl- -> [CoCl4]2- + 6H2O.

questions.question: Explain why the shape of the cobalt complex ion changes when concentrated HCl is added.
questions.answer: Chloride ions are larger than water, so only four can fit around Co2+; the complex changes from octahedral to tetrahedral.
steps: [Co(H2O)6]2+ is octahedral with six small water ligands.
[CoCl4]2- has four larger chloride ligands.
Steric repulsion means only four chloride ligands fit, so the shape becomes tetrahedral.

questions.question: Describe the reactions of aqueous cobalt(II) sulfate with NaOH(aq), excess NH3(aq) and concentrated HCl, linking each to an equation (no state symbols).
questions.answer: NaOH: blue Co(OH)2 precipitate; excess NH3: precipitate dissolves to a brown solution; conc HCl: pink to blue [CoCl4]2-.
steps: NaOH: Co2+ + 2OH- -> Co(OH)2 gives a blue precipitate, insoluble in excess.
Excess NH3 first forms the same blue precipitate, Co2+ + 2OH- -> Co(OH)2.
Excess NH3 then dissolves it: Co(OH)2 + 6NH3 -> [Co(NH3)6]2+ + 2OH-, which air oxidises to a brown solution.
Conc HCl: [Co(H2O)6]2+ + 4Cl- -> [CoCl4]2- + 6H2O, pink to blue.
Each reaction is a precipitation or ligand exchange.

questions.question: Excess sodium thiosulfate is added to ammonium vanadate(V). What colour is the final mixture? A yellow, B blue, C green, D violet.
questions.answer: C - green (V3+ formed)
steps: Thiosulfate reduces V(V) (yellow) to V(IV) (blue VO2+) and then to V(III).
With excess thiosulfate the final species is V3+, which is green.
So the answer is C.

questions.question: Which reagent added to aqueous sodium dichromate(VI) shifts the equilibrium to form a yellow solution? A NaOH(aq), B HCl(aq), C Zn(s), D H2O2(aq).
questions.answer: A - NaOH(aq)
steps: Dichromate: Cr2O7 2- + H2O <=> 2CrO4 2- + 2H+ (orange to yellow).
Adding alkali removes H+, shifting the equilibrium to the right.
Yellow chromate(VI) ions are formed, so the answer is A.

questions.question: Explain the highest stable oxidation state of vanadium by referring to its electronic configuration.
questions.answer: +5, because all five outer electrons (4s2 3d3) can be lost, giving a stable 3d0 configuration.
steps: Vanadium is [Ar] 3d3 4s2, with five electrons in the 3d and 4s subshells.
Losing all five gives V5+, which is [Ar] 3d0.
A d0 configuration has no electrons to remove further, so +5 is the highest stable state.

questions.question: Justify using sodium thiosulfate to convert VO2+ into V3+ by writing equations and calculating E-zero values from the given table and Data Booklet.
questions.answer: 2VO2+ + 4H+ + 2S2O3 2- -> 2V3+ + 2H2O + S4O6 2- has E-zero(cell) = +0.25 V (feasible); the further reduction 2V3+ + 2S2O3 2- -> 2V2+ + S4O6 2- has E-zero(cell) = -0.35 V (not feasible), so V3+ is the final product.
steps: Data Booklet: S4O6 2- + 2e- <=> 2S2O3 2- has E-zero = +0.09 V; thiosulfate is the reductant (oxidised to S4O6 2-).
VO2+ to V3+: 2VO2+ + 4H+ + 2S2O3 2- -> 2V3+ + 2H2O + S4O6 2-; E-zero(cell) = +0.34 - (+0.09) = +0.25 V, positive so feasible.
V3+ to V2+: 2V3+ + 2S2O3 2- -> 2V2+ + S4O6 2-; E-zero(cell) = -0.26 - (+0.09) = -0.35 V, negative so not feasible.
So thiosulfate reduces VO2+ to V3+ but not further, with no other vanadium species formed.

questions.question: Explain why nickel is not a suitable reagent to convert VO2+ into V3+ with no other vanadium species formed.
questions.answer: Ni (E-zero = -0.25 V) is a strong enough reductant to reduce VO2+ to V3+, but for V3+ to V2+ the E-zero(cell) is -0.26 - (-0.25) = -0.01 V, which is almost zero, so reduction can go on to V2+ and a mixture of vanadium species forms.
steps: Data Booklet: Ni2+ + 2e- <=> Ni has E-zero = -0.25 V.
VO2+ to V3+: E-zero(cell) = +0.34 - (-0.25) = +0.59 V, so Ni reduces VO2+ readily.
V3+ to V2+: E-zero(cell) = -0.26 - (-0.25) = -0.01 V, which is so close to zero that this step is not clearly infeasible, so some V2+ can form.
Therefore Ni cannot give V3+ only, unlike thiosulfate (which has E-zero(cell) of -0.35 V for the second step).

questions.question: Give the colour of the solution at the end-point of the potassium manganate(VII) titration.
questions.answer: Pale pink (purple) at the end-point
steps: Excess MnO4- gives a persistent pale pink to purple colour.
The end-point is when all Fe2+ has been oxidised.

questions.question: Suggest why the VO2+ ions formed do not affect the manganate(VII) titration.
questions.answer: Fe2+ (E-zero +0.77 V) is a stronger reducing agent than VO2+ (VO3-/VO2+ system, +1.00 V), so MnO4- oxidises Fe2+ first and the end-point is reached before VO2+ reacts.
steps: From the table, VO3- + 4H+ + e- <=> VO2+ + 2H2O has E-zero = +1.00 V, which is more positive than Fe3+/Fe2+ at +0.77 V.
A more positive E-zero means a weaker reducing agent, so VO2+ is a weaker reductant than Fe2+.
MnO4- therefore oxidises all the Fe2+ first, and the first permanent pink colour marks the Fe2+ end-point.
VO2+ is only oxidised after the Fe2+ is used up, so it does not change the volume of MnO4- measured.

questions.question: A 4.87 g ferrovanadium sample is dissolved and the vanadium reacted with 25.0 cm3 of 0.250 mol dm-3 Fe2+; the remaining Fe2+ is titrated with 22.50 cm3 of 0.0195 mol dm-3 MnO4- (1:5 with Fe2+). Find the percentage by mass of V.
questions.answer: 42.4% vanadium by mass
steps: Total Fe2+ added = 0.250 x 0.0250 = 6.25 x 10^-3 mol.
Fe2+ reacted with V = 6.25 x 10^-3 - 2.19 x 10^-3 = 4.06 x 10^-3 mol (1:1 with VO2+ in the aliquot).
Vanadium in the whole 250.0 cm3 = 4.06 x 10^-3 x 10 = 4.06 x 10^-2 mol.

questions.question: Write two equations showing a possible mechanism for V2O5 catalysing 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3 (no state symbols).
steps: Step 1: V2O5 oxidises SO2 and is itself reduced to V2O4: SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + V2O4.
Step 2: O2 reoxidises V2O4 back to V2O5: V2O4 + 1/2 O2 -> V2O5.
Adding gives 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3 with V2O5 unchanged.

questions.question: The Pt(NH3)2Cl2 complex used in cancer treatment corresponds to which of three structures X, Y, Z? (Structures are diagrams.)
questions.answer: A: structure X only
steps: Cisplatin is the cis isomer of square planar Pt(NH3)2Cl2, with the two Cl on the same side (adjacent, 90 degrees apart).
X is square planar with Cl next to Cl (cis); Y is square planar with Cl diagonally opposite Cl (trans), which is not the drug.
Z is tetrahedral and has no cis or trans forms, so the drug is X only.

questions.question: Which transition metal complex is commonly used as a cancer treatment? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: C: the square planar cis-Pt(NH3)2Cl2 (cisplatin)
steps: Cisplatin is cis-diamminedichloroplatinum(II): a square planar Pt(II) complex with Cl next to Cl.
C shows the two Cl on the same side (cis); D shows Cl diagonally opposite (trans-platin), which is not used in treatment.
The copper complexes A and B are tetrahedral and are not cancer drugs.

questions.question: In the mechanism Ag+ + Ce4+ -> Ag2+ + Ce3+; Ti+ + Ag2+ -> Ti2+ + Ag+; Ti2+ + Ce4+ -> Ti3+ + Ce3+, which statement is correct? A Ce4+ catalyses Ag+ oxidation, B Ti2+ catalyses Ag+, C Ag+ catalyses Ti+ oxidation, D Ag2+ catalyses Ti+.
questions.answer: C - the oxidation of Ti+ is catalysed by Ag+ ions
steps: Ag+ is consumed in step 1 and regenerated in step 2.
Ag+ is therefore a catalyst, and the reaction it speeds up is oxidation of Ti+.
Ag2+ is an intermediate, not a catalyst.

questions.question: Zinc is not classified as a transition element because: A the 3d subshell of zinc is full, B zinc forms only one stable ion, C the only stable zinc ion is [Ar] 3d10, D neither zinc nor its ions show catalytic properties.
questions.answer: C - the only stable zinc ion has configuration [Ar] 3d10
steps: A transition element must form ions with a partly filled d subshell.
Zn2+ is [Ar] 3d10, which is full, so zinc does not meet the definition.
Option C gives this reason most directly.

questions.question: State the colour of each chromium species in the titration reaction (Cr2O7 2- and Cr3+).
questions.answer: Cr2O7 2-: orange; Cr3+: green
steps: Dichromate(VI) ions are orange in acid.
Chromium(III) ions are green.

questions.question: Suggest a reason why an indicator is needed in this titration.
questions.answer: It shows the end-point by a sharp colour change when all Fe2+ has been used.
steps: The reactants are colourless or pale, so the endpoint cannot be seen without an indicator.
The indicator gives an intense colour change at the equivalence point.

questions.question: A 50.0 g cement sample gives 100.0 cm3 solution; 50.0 cm3 titrated with 10.90 cm3 of 3.24 x 10^-4 mol dm-3 ammonium iron(II) sulfate. Find the percentage by mass of K2Cr2O7 (Mr 294.2) in the cement.
questions.answer: 6.93 x 10^-4 % K2Cr2O7 by mass
steps: Dichromate = Fe2+ / 6 = 5.89 x 10^-7 mol in the 50.0 cm3 aliquot.
Dichromate in 100.0 cm3 = 2 x 5.89 x 10^-7 = 1.18 x 10^-6 mol.

questions.question: Explain why N-phenylanthranilic acid is dissolved in NaOH before mixing with water.
questions.answer: The acid is insoluble in water but dissolves in NaOH by forming a soluble sodium salt.
steps: The acid is an organic acid with low solubility in water.
Reaction with NaOH forms its soluble sodium salt.
Dissolving it this way allows it to be diluted with water to make the indicator.

questions.question: Describe how DPC acts as a bidentate ligand, using its structure to show the atoms involved.
questions.answer: DPC is bidentate because it has two donor atoms with lone pairs (the C=O oxygen and an adjacent N-H nitrogen), each forming a dative covalent bond to Cr(VI); three DPC give six bonds, so the complex is octahedral.
steps: A bidentate ligand donates two lone pairs from two different atoms to the same metal ion.
In DPC the oxygen of the C=O group has lone pairs, and the nitrogen atoms of the N-H groups also have lone pairs.
One O (or N) and an N atom, positioned so a chelate ring can form, each donate a lone pair to Cr6+ by dative covalent bonds.
Three DPC ligands give 3 x 2 = 6 dative bonds, which is why Cr(DPC)3 6+ is octahedral.

questions.question: Suggest why the colour of the chromium(VI) complex is not due to electron transfer between split d-orbitals.
questions.answer: Chromium(VI) is d0, so it has no d electrons to be promoted between split d levels.
steps: Cr(VI) is 3d0 with no electrons in d orbitals.
A d-d transition needs electrons in d orbitals, so it cannot occur.
The colour comes from ligand-to-metal charge transfer instead.

questions.question: Explain in terms of entropy why the dimethylglyoxime complex formation is favoured.
questions.answer: The number of particles increases from 5 to 7, so entropy increases.
steps: Left side: [Ni(H2O)6]2+, 2 dimethylglyoxime, 2 OH-, i.e. 5 species.
Right side: the complex plus 6 H2O, i.e. 7 species.
More particles means a more positive entropy change, which favours the reaction.

questions.question: The bonding within [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ is: A covalent, dative covalent and ionic, B covalent and dative covalent only, C covalent only, D dative covalent only.
questions.answer: B - covalent and dative covalent only
steps: Bonds within each NH3 and H2O are covalent.
Ligand-to-metal bonds are dative covalent.
There is no separate counter-ion in the complex ion, so no ionic bonds.

questions.question: Which complex is tetrahedral? A [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], B [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2], C [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+, D [CoCl4]2-.
questions.answer: D - [CoCl4]2-
steps: Four-coordinate complexes are tetrahedral or square planar.
Pt(NH3)2Cl2 is square planar, and the Cu complexes are octahedral (6 ligands).
[CoCl4]2- has four ligands and is tetrahedral.

questions.question: Which complex contains a bidentate ligand? A [Co(NH2CH2CH2NHCH2CH2NH2)2]3+, B [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+, C [Ni(NH2CH2CH2NH2)3]2+, D [Mn(EDTA)]2-.
questions.answer: C - [Ni(NH2CH2CH2NH2)3]2+ (en is bidentate)
steps: NH2CH2CH2NH2 (en) has two N donor atoms, so it is bidentate.
NH2CH2CH2NHCH2CH2NH2 is tridentate and EDTA is hexadentate.
NH3 and H2O are monodentate, so only option C has a bidentate ligand.

questions.question: Which ion is not blue? A VO2+, B [Co(H2O)6]2+, C [Cr(H2O)6]2+, D [Cu(H2O)6]2+.
questions.answer: B - [Co(H2O)6]2+ (pink)
steps: VO2+ (vanadyl, V(IV)) is blue.
[Cr(H2O)6]2+ and [Cu(H2O)6]2+ are blue.
[Co(H2O)6]2+ is pink, so it is the ion that is not blue.

questions.question: In which species does the transition metal have the lowest oxidation number? A [Cu(NH3)2]+, B [Fe(CN)6]3-, C MnSO4, D Ni(CO)4.
questions.answer: D - Ni(CO)4 (Ni is 0)
steps: [Cu(NH3)2]+: Cu is +1.
[Fe(CN)6]3-: Fe is +3.
MnSO4: Mn is +2.
Ni(CO)4: CO is neutral, so Ni is 0, the lowest.

questions.question: State the oxidation number of vanadium in Na3VO4.
steps: Na is +1, so the VO4 3- unit has a charge of -3.

questions.question: Explain why vanadium(V) does not exist as [V(H2O)6]5+ in aqueous solution.
questions.answer: V5+ is small and highly charged, so it polarises water strongly and forms oxo ions such as VO2+ instead of [V(H2O)6]5+.
steps: V5+ is small with a very high charge, so its charge density is very high.
It polarises the O-H bonds of the coordinated water strongly.
The water loses H+, and V-O bonds form, giving oxo ions such as [VO2(H2O)4]+.

questions.topic: Empirical And Molecular Formula Hydrated Salt
questions.question: Hydrated potassium vanadium(III) sulfate contains 7.9% K, 10.2% V, 12.9% S, 4.8% H, 64.2% O. Calculate the empirical formula and write the overall formula with K+, V3+, sulfate and water.
steps: Divide each % by its Ar: K 0.202, V 0.200, S 0.402, H 4.76, O 4.01 (mol per 100 g).
Divide by the smallest (0.200): K 1, V 1, S 2, H 24, O 20.
Empirical unit: KVS2H24O20, which means KV(SO4)2 with 12 H2O.
Charges check: K+ + V3+ = 2 x SO4 2- (+4 = -4).
Formula: KV(SO4)2.12H2O.

questions.question: Calculate the ratio of moles of MnO4- to moles of V3+, given 10.0 cm3 of 0.132 mol dm-3 V3+ titrated with 26.40 cm3 of 0.0200 mol dm-3 MnO4- in acid.
Write the equation for the reaction between manganate(VII) and vanadium(III) ions in acid (no state symbols).
steps: Mn changes from +7 to +2 (5 e- per MnO4-); V changes from +3 to +5 (2 e- per V).
Use a 2:5 ratio to balance electrons (10 e- each side).
Balance O with water and H with H+: 2MnO4- + 5V3+ + 2H2O -> 2Mn2+ + 5VO2+ + 4H+.
Check charges: left -2 + 15 = +13; right +4 (Mn2+) + 5 (VO2+) + 4 (H+) = +13.

questions.topic: Reduction Of Vanadium Using Fe And Sn
questions.question: Compare and contrast the use of iron and tin to reduce vanadium(V) step by step in acid, with equations and E-zero values from the tables only.
questions.answer: Both iron and tin reduce VO2+ to VO2+ and then to V3+ (all E-zero(cell) values positive). Iron goes one step further, reducing V3+ to V2+ (E-zero(cell) = +0.18 V), but tin cannot (E-zero(cell) = -0.12 V), so tin stops at V3+.
steps: Iron step 3: 2V3+ + Fe -> 2V2+ + Fe2+, E-zero(cell) = -0.26 - (-0.44) = +0.18 V, feasible, so iron reduces vanadium all the way to V2+.
Tin step 3: 2V3+ + Sn -> 2V2+ + Sn2+, E-zero(cell) = -0.26 - (-0.14) = -0.12 V, not feasible, so tin stops at V3+.
Similarity: both give VO2+ then V3+ with positive E-zero(cell); difference: iron gives V2+ as the final product, tin gives V3+.

questions.question: Which complex contains only monodentate ligands? A [Fe(CN)6]4-, B [Cr(C2O4)3]3-, C [Ni(EDTA)]2-, D [Co(NH2CH2CH2NH2)2Cl2].
steps: CN- donates through one atom, so it is monodentate.
C2O4 2- is bidentate, EDTA is hexadentate, and en is bidentate.
So only A contains only monodentate ligands.

questions.question: Which metal hydroxide precipitate is soluble in both excess aqueous ammonia and excess NaOH? A Cu(OH)2, B Fe(OH)2, C Ni(OH)2, D Zn(OH)2.
questions.answer: D - Zn(OH)2
steps: Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric, so it dissolves in excess NaOH.
It also dissolves in excess NH3 by forming [Zn(NH3)4]2+.
Cu(OH)2 and Ni(OH)2 dissolve in NH3 only, and Fe(OH)2 dissolves in neither.

questions.question: Explain why mercury is classified as a d-block element but is not a transition element.
questions.answer: Hg is a d-block element because its last electron fills the 5d subshell, but Hg and its common ions have a full 5d10 subshell, so it is not a transition element.
steps: Mercury's configuration [Xe] 4f14 5d10 6s2 puts it in the d block as the 5d subshell is being filled.
A transition element must form an ion with a partly filled d subshell.
Hg2+ has a 5d10 configuration, which is full.
So Hg does not meet the definition and is not a transition element.

questions.question: Explain, using oxidation numbers, why Hg + HNO3 -> Hg(NO3)2 + NO + H2O is a redox reaction.
questions.answer: Hg is oxidised from 0 to +2 and N is reduced from +5 (in HNO3) to +2 (in NO).
steps: In Hg (element) the oxidation number is 0; in Hg(NO3)2 it is +2, so Hg is oxidised.
In HNO3 the nitrogen is +5; in NO it is +2, so N is reduced.
Both oxidation and reduction occur, so it is a redox reaction.

questions.question: Deduce the ionic half-equations for the mercury and nitric acid reaction (no state symbols).
steps: Oxidation: Hg -> Hg2+ + 2e-.
Reduction: NO3- + 4H+ + 3e- -> NO + 2H2O.
Check: electrons balance after multiplying to 6 e- each.

questions.question: Complete the equation by adding stoichiometric coefficients: Hg(l) + HNO3(aq) -> Hg(NO3)2(aq) + NO(g) + H2O(l).
questions.answer: 3Hg(l) + 8HNO3(aq) -> 3Hg(NO3)2(aq) + 2NO(g) + 4H2O(l)
steps: Electrons: 3 Hg each lose 2 e- = 6 e-; 2 NO each gain 3 e- = 6 e-.
Balance Hg: 3 on each side.
Balance N: 6 in Hg(NO3)2 + 2 in NO = 8 HNO3.
Balance H: 8 H on left = 4 H2O on right.

questions.question: Write the equation for one mole of Hg(NO3)2 reacting with ethanol to form mercury(II) fulminate, Hg(CNO)2, with ethanal and water as other products.
questions.answer: Hg(NO3)2 + 3C2H5OH -> Hg(CNO)2 + 2CH3CHO + 5H2O
steps: Write the products as Hg(CNO)2, CH3CHO and H2O, with one Hg(NO3)2 as stated.
Balance C: Hg(CNO)2 has 2 C and each CH3CHO has 2 C, so 3 ethanol (6 C) gives 2 C + 2 x 2 C.
Balance H: 3C2H5OH has 18 H; 2CH3CHO has 8 H, so 10 H goes into 5H2O.
Check O: left 6 (nitrate) + 3 (ethanol) = 9; right 2 (CNO) + 2 (ethanal) + 5 (water) = 9. N and Hg also balance.

questions.question: Calculate the total volume of gas, in cm3, produced when 1.00 g of Hg(CNO)2 decomposes at room temperature and pressure. Equation: 3Hg(CNO)2 -> Hg(CN)2 + 2Hg + 2CO2 + 2CO + 2N2.
questions.answer: 169 cm3 (about 1.69 x 10^2 cm3)
steps: Gas per 3 mol Hg(CNO)2 = 2 CO2 + 2 CO + 2 N2 = 6 mol; so 2 mol gas per mol Hg(CNO)2.
Volume at RTP (24.0 dm3 mol-1) = 7.03 x 10^-3 x 24000 = 169 cm3.

questions.question: Suggest why KCl crystals are needed in the outer tube of the calomel electrode.
questions.answer: To keep the solution saturated so the chloride ion concentration stays constant and the electrode potential is fixed.
steps: The calomel half-cell depends on the chloride ion concentration.
Excess KCl crystals keep the solution saturated, so [Cl-] stays constant.
A constant [Cl-] gives a constant, reproducible electrode potential.

questions.question: A calomel electrode gives a voltmeter reading of +0.37 V against the Sn2+(aq)|Sn(s) half-cell. Deduce the E-zero value of Sn2+|Sn.
questions.answer: E-zero(Sn2+|Sn) = -0.13 V
steps: The voltmeter shows the cell emf: the calomel electrode is the positive terminal and Sn is the negative terminal.
E-zero(cell) = E-zero(positive) - E-zero(negative) = (+0.24) - E-zero(Sn2+|Sn) = +0.37 V.

questions.question: Write the overall equation for the cell reaction of the calomel and Sn2+/Sn cell.
questions.answer: Hg2Cl2 + Sn -> 2Hg + 2Cl- + Sn2+ (with states: Hg2Cl2(s) + Sn(s) -> 2Hg(l) + 2Cl-(aq) + Sn2+(aq))
steps: The calomel electrode is the positive electrode, so reduction occurs: Hg2Cl2 + 2e- -> 2Hg + 2Cl-.
Sn is the negative electrode, so oxidation occurs: Sn -> Sn2+ + 2e-.
Add the two half-equations; the 2 electrons cancel to give Hg2Cl2 + Sn -> 2Hg + 2Cl- + Sn2+.

questions.question: Add labels to complete the diagram of a standard hydrogen electrode, including details of essential conditions.
questions.answer: Top box (gas inlet): hydrogen gas at 100 kPa (1 atm); middle box (the electrode): platinum electrode (coated with platinum black); bottom box (the solution): 1.00 mol dm-3 H+(aq) (e.g. HCl), all at 298 K.
steps: The gas entering at the top is hydrogen, H2(g), at a pressure of 100 kPa (1 atm).
The electrode is platinum (platinum-coated, inert), which lets H2 and H+ exchange electrons and acts as the catalyst surface.
The solution is aqueous acid with an H+ concentration of 1.00 mol dm-3 (e.g. hydrochloric acid).
The temperature must be 298 K; these are the standard conditions for the SHE, which is defined as 0.00 V.

questions.question: Suggest one advantage of using a calomel electrode in place of a standard hydrogen electrode.
questions.answer: It is easier and safer to use because it needs no hydrogen gas or platinum set-up.
steps: The SHE needs hydrogen gas at 1 atm and 1 mol dm-3 H+, which is hard to control.
The calomel electrode is a simple, stable solid-liquid system at room conditions.
So it is easier and more convenient to use as a reference.

questions.question: Which complex has a ligand-metal-ligand bond angle of 109.5 degrees? A [CuCl4]2-, B [Fe(EDTA)]-, C [Ag(NH3)2]+, D [Pt(NH3)2Cl2].
questions.answer: A - [CuCl4]2- (tetrahedral)
steps: A tetrahedral complex has bond angles of 109.5 degrees.
[CuCl4]2- is tetrahedral.
[Ag(NH3)2]+ is linear (180), [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] is square planar (90 and 180), and [Fe(EDTA)]- is octahedral (90).

questions.question: Which is the equation for the reaction when a small amount of aqueous ammonia is added to zinc ions? (Options not in text.)
steps: With a small amount of NH3, ammonia acts as a base and removes two H+ from coordinated water (deprotonation).
This gives the neutral, insoluble white precipitate Zn(OH)2(H2O)4 and NH4+, option B.
Options C and D show ligand exchange to the ammine complex, which only happens in excess ammonia (A is a charged soluble ion, not a precipitate).

questions.question: Which electronic configuration is correct? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: D: Cu is [Ar] 3d10 4s1
steps: Copper is an exception: a full 3d subshell (3d10) is more stable, so one 4s electron moves to 3d, giving [Ar] 3d10 4s1.
A is wrong because Ti2+ is [Ar] 3d2 (4s electrons are lost first); B is wrong because Cr is [Ar] 3d5 4s1; C is wrong because Fe3+ is [Ar] 3d5.

questions.question: What is the coordination number of chromium in Cr2(CH3CO2)4(H2O)2? Options: A two, B four, C six, D twelve. (Structure is a diagram.)
questions.answer: C: six
steps: Each chromium is bonded to four oxygen atoms from four different bridging ethanoate ligands.
It also bonds to one water molecule and to the other chromium atom (Cr-Cr bond).
So each Cr has 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 bonds, giving a coordination number of six.

questions.question: What is the sequence of oxidation number changes for vanadium when V2O5 is used in the Contact Process? A +2 +1 +2, B +2 +5 +2, C +5 +4 +5, D +5 +6 +5.
steps: V2O5 contains V(V) = +5.
It is reduced to V(IV) (+4) by SO2.
It is reoxidised back to V(V) (+5) by O2.

questions.question: A compound contains 39.5% K, 28.2% Fe and 32.3% O by mass. Calculate its empirical formula.
questions.answer: K2FeO4
steps: Empirical formula K2FeO4.

questions.question: Give a reason why the activation energy for the iodide and peroxodisulfate reaction is high without a catalyst.
questions.answer: Both reacting ions are negatively charged, so they repel each other and few collisions have enough energy.
steps: I- and S2O8 2- are both negative ions.
They repel each other, so the collision needs a lot of energy to overcome this.
So the activation energy is high.

questions.question: Write the ionic equations for the reactions that occur when Fe2+ catalyst is added (no state symbols).
steps: Fe2+ is oxidised by peroxodisulfate: 2Fe2+ + S2O8 2- -> 2Fe3+ + 2SO4 2-.
Fe3+ oxidises iodide and is reduced back: 2Fe3+ + 2I- -> 2Fe2+ + I2.

questions.question: Explain how water acts as a monodentate ligand in [Fe(H2O)6]2+.
questions.answer: Each water molecule donates one lone pair from O to Fe2+, forming one dative covalent bond.
steps: The oxygen atom in H2O has two lone pairs.
One lone pair is donated to an empty orbital on Fe2+, forming a dative covalent bond.
Only one donor atom per water, so it is monodentate.

questions.question: Explain the shape of the [Fe(H2O)6]2+ complex ion.
questions.answer: Six ligands bonded to Fe2+ arrange as far apart as possible, giving an octahedral shape with bond angles of 90 degrees.
steps: Six bonding pairs around the central Fe2+ repel each other equally.
They arrange to minimise repulsion, giving an octahedron.
All bond angles are 90 degrees.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of the iron(II) complex, why carbon monoxide is toxic.
questions.answer: CO binds to Fe2+ in haem more strongly than O2, so it blocks O2 from binding and stops oxygen transport.
steps: CO forms a stronger dative bond to Fe2+ in the haem group than O2 does.
The strong binding is hard to reverse.
So CO occupies the site that O2 needs, and oxygen transport is blocked.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of entropy, why the reaction of ethanedioate ions with iron(II) ions in aqueous solution is feasible.
questions.answer: Each ethanedioate replaces water ligands, so the number of particles increases and the entropy increases.
steps: Ethanedioate (C2O4 2-) is bidentate and displaces water ligands from [Fe(H2O)6]2+.
Each ligand replaces water ligands, so the water released increases the number of particles.
A positive entropy change makes the reaction feasible.

questions.question: Solution Y contains 6.28 g dm-3 of iron as Fe2+ and Fe3+. 25.0 cm3 of Y titrated with 2.56 g dm-3 dichromate, mean titre 22.55 cm3. Find the percentage of iron present as Fe3+.
questions.answer: About 58% of the iron is Fe3+
steps: Dichromate concentration = 2.56 / 294.2 = 8.70 x 10^-3 mol dm-3.
Moles dichromate = 8.70 x 10^-3 x 0.02255 = 1.96 x 10^-4 mol.

questions.question: What is the coordination number of chromium(III) in [CrCl2(NH2CH2CH2NH2)2]x? Options: A 2, B 3, C 4, D 6.
steps: 2 chloride ligands each give 1 bond = 2.
2 bidentate en ligands each give 2 bonds = 4.
Total = 6.

questions.question: What is the overall charge of [CrCl2(NH2CH2CH2NH2)2]x? Options: A 0, B +1, C +2, D +3.
steps: Cr is +3.
Two Cl- give -2, and the en ligands are neutral.
Overall charge = +3 - 2 = +1.

questions.question: Which complex ion is square planar? A [Cu(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+, B [CuCl4]2-, C [Pt(NH3)2Cl2], D [Ag(NH3)2]+.
questions.answer: C - [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]
steps: Pt2+ is d8 and forms square planar complexes with four ligands.
[CuCl4]2- is tetrahedral in the usual description.
So option C is square planar.

questions.question: Which copper complex ion is colourless? A [CuCl2]-, B [CuCl4]2-, C [Cu(H2O)6]2+, D [Cu(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+.
questions.answer: A - [CuCl2]- (copper(I), d10)
steps: [CuCl2]- contains Cu(I), which is 3d10 with no d-d transitions.
The other three contain Cu(II), which has a partly filled d9 and is coloured.

questions.question: Which complex ion includes a bond angle of 107 degrees? A [Cr(NH3)6]3+, B [CuCl2]-, C [CuCl4]2-, D [Cr(H2O)6]2+.
questions.answer: A - [Cr(NH3)6]3+ (H-N-H angle of NH3 is about 107 degrees)
steps: NH3 is pyramidal with H-N-H bond angles of about 107 degrees.
Option A contains NH3 ligands; B (180), C (109.5) and D (90) do not give 107.
So the answer is A.

questions.question: Which complex ion is colourless? A [Al(H2O)6]3+, B [Cu(H2O)6]2+, C [Fe(H2O)6]3+, D [Ni(H2O)6]2+.
steps: Al3+ has no d electrons (3d0).
No d-d transitions are possible, so it is colourless.
The other ions are d-block and coloured.

questions.question: Which diagram shows the change in relative colour intensity when EDTA4- is added to chromium(III) ions?
questions.answer: C: peak at 0.001 mol of ligand, higher than the cyanide peak (about 7.7), then falling gradually
steps: The CN- graph peaks at 0.006 mol ligand for 0.001 mol Cr3+, i.e. a 6:1 ratio, giving [Cr(CN)6]3-.
EDTA4- is hexadentate, so one ion wraps round Cr3+ and the complex forms in a 1:1 ratio: the maximum colour intensity is at 0.001 mol EDTA4-.
The EDTA complex has a greater colour intensity than the CN- one, so the peak must be higher than 6 (about 7.7).
Only graph C has its peak at 0.001 mol and a maximum above 6; after the peak the intensity falls as the solution is diluted by added reagent.

questions.question: Acidified manganate(VII) ions react with ethanedioate ions. Which statement is correct? (Question text and options missing.)
questions.answer: B: Mn2+ acts as a catalyst (rate increases); concentration of reactants decreases (rate decreases)
steps: Mn2+ is a product that catalyses the reaction (autocatalysis), so the rate increases as Mn2+ builds up.
Later the rate falls because the reactants MnO4- and C2O4 2- are used up, so their concentrations decrease.
MnO4- is a reactant, not a catalyst, and the kinetic energy of particles does not fall because the temperature stays the same.

questions.question: What is the coordination number of chromium in the complex ion shown? Options: A 2, B 3, C 4, D 6. (Structure is a diagram.)
steps: The complex is [CrCl2(en)2]+: each ethane-1,2-diamine (en) ligand is bidentate and donates two lone pairs from its two N atoms.
Four N bonds from two en ligands plus two Cl- bonds give 4 + 2 = 6 dative bonds to Cr.
So the coordination number is 6 (octahedral).

questions.question: Aqueous NaOH and aqueous NH3 are added in excess to separate portions of pale green solution E. Which ion is present? A Cu2+, B Fe2+, C Ni2+, D V2+.
questions.answer: B - Fe2+
steps: Pale green aqueous solution suggests Fe2+ ([Fe(H2O)6]2+).
Cu2+ is blue, Ni2+ is green and dissolves in excess NH3, V2+ is violet.
Fe(OH)2 precipitate does not dissolve in excess NaOH or NH3.
So the ion is Fe2+.

questions.question: Aqueous ammonia is added in excess to aqueous Cu2+. What is the overall equation? (Options not in text.)
steps: In excess ammonia, NH3 replaces four of the six water ligands (ligand exchange), forming the deep blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+.
Four NH3 enter and four H2O leave, giving 4H2O as a product; the charge stays 2+, so this is option C.
A is the first step (small amount of ammonia, precipitate), and B and D do not match the 4:4 exchange of the observed ion.

questions.question: Which equation shows a redox reaction in which the solution turns yellow? (Equation options not in text.)
questions.answer: D: 2Cr(OH)3 + 3H2O2 + 4KOH -> 2K2CrO4 + 8H2O
steps: In D Cr changes from +3 in Cr(OH)3 to +6 in K2CrO4, so it is oxidised, and O in H2O2 (-1) is reduced to -2; this is redox and the yellow chromate(VI) forms.
A is redox but gives a pale green solution of FeCl2; B (VO3- to VO2+ in acid) and C (Cr2O7 2- to CrO4 2-) have no change in oxidation number, so they are not redox.

questions.question: Which is a d-block element but not a transition element? A cobalt, B copper, C nickel, D zinc.
questions.answer: D - zinc
steps: Zinc is in the d block but its ion Zn2+ is 3d10 (full).
Cobalt, copper and nickel all form ions with partly filled d subshells.
So zinc is d-block but not a transition element.

questions.question: Which equation shows the formation of a precipitate? (Options not in text.)
steps: A precipitate is an uncharged (neutral) hydroxide complex, which is insoluble in water.
In A the soluble zincate ion [Zn(OH)4]2- is protonated to the neutral [Zn(H2O)4(OH)2] = Zn(OH)2, which precipitates.
In B, C and D an insoluble neutral hydroxide or a metal ion converts into a soluble charged ion, so these are dissolving, not precipitating.

questions.question: In Cu + 4H+ + 2NO3- -> Cu2+ + NO2 + 2H2O, identify the element oxidised and the element reduced, with oxidation numbers.
questions.answer: Cu is oxidised (0 to +2); N is reduced (+5 to +4).
steps: Cu goes from 0 in the element to +2 in Cu2+, so Cu is oxidised.
N goes from +5 in NO3- to +4 in NO2, so N is reduced.

questions.question: Suggest one precaution, other than gloves, goggles and lab coats, when reacting copper with concentrated nitric acid, clearly stating the hazard.
questions.answer: Carry out the reaction in a fume cupboard, because toxic NO2 gas is produced.
steps: The reaction gives off brown NO2 gas, which is toxic.
Precaution: use a fume cupboard to remove the gas.
State the hazard: NO2 is toxic if inhaled.

questions.question: A 5.000 g sample of Prince's metal is dissolved and diluted to 250 cm3. 10.0 cm3 aliquots are titrated with 0.100 mol dm-3 thiosulfate; mean titre 22.65 cm3. Calculate the percentage of copper by mass.
steps: Moles thiosulfate = 0.100 x 0.02265 = 2.265 x 10^-3 mol.
Cu2+ : I2 = 2 : 1, so moles Cu2+ in 10.0 cm3 = 2.265 x 10^-3 mol.

questions.question: Describe the observations when NaOH is added drop by drop (to excess) to separate Cu2+ and Zn2+ solutions, with ionic equations and state symbols.
questions.answer: Cu2+: blue precipitate, insoluble in excess. Zn2+: white precipitate, dissolves in excess to colourless solution.
steps: Cu2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) -> Cu(OH)2(s): a pale blue precipitate forms.
Excess NaOH does not dissolve Cu(OH)2, so the precipitate remains.
Zn2+(aq) + 2OH-(aq) -> Zn(OH)2(s): a white precipitate forms.
Zn(OH)2(s) + 2OH-(aq) -> [Zn(OH)4]2-(aq): the precipitate dissolves in excess to a colourless solution.
So Zn(OH)2 is amphoteric and Cu(OH)2 is not.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of electronic configurations, why copper is a transition element but zinc is not.
questions.answer: Cu2+ is 3d9 (partly filled d subshell), but Zn2+ is 3d10 (full), so only Cu is a transition element.
steps: Copper forms Cu2+ ions with configuration [Ar] 3d9, which is partly filled.
Zinc forms Zn2+ with [Ar] 3d10, which is full.
A transition element must form ions with a partly filled d subshell, so only copper qualifies.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of structure, why brass is less malleable than pure copper.
questions.answer: Zinc atoms of different size distort the regular layers of copper atoms, so the layers cannot slide easily.
steps: Pure copper has regular layers of atoms that slide over each other.
Zn atoms are a different size and disrupt the layers.
The layers are less able to slide, so brass is less malleable.

questions.question: Which vanadium ion is yellow in aqueous solution? A VO2+, B VO2+ (dioxovanadium(V)), C V3+, D V2+.
questions.answer: B - VO2+ (dioxovanadium(V), yellow)
steps: VO2+ (dioxovanadium(V)) is the yellow V(V) ion.
The vanadyl ion (VO2+, V(IV)) is blue.
V3+ is green and V2+ is violet.

questions.question: Explain the shape of [Ag(NH3)2]+.
questions.answer: Linear, with an NH3-Ag-NH3 bond angle of 180 degrees.
steps: Ag+ has two bonding pairs (two dative bonds from NH3).
Two bonding pairs repel each other as far apart as possible.
This gives a linear shape with a 180 degree angle.

questions.question: Explain why [Ag(NH3)2]+ is colourless.
questions.answer: Ag+ is 4d10 (full d subshell), so no d-d transitions are possible.
steps: Ag+ has a full d subshell (4d10).
No electron can be promoted between split d levels.
So no visible light is absorbed and the ion is colourless.

questions.question: Complete the equation for the reaction of C6H12O6 (glucose) with [Ag(NH3)2]+ in alkali, forming silver and an organic compound Y (C6H12O7) plus two other products.
steps: Glucose is oxidised to C6H12O7 (gluconic acid), so Ag+ is reduced to Ag.
Two Ag+ are needed to gain two electrons.
Ammonia is released from the complex, and the alkali supplies OH-.
Balance: C 6, H 26, O 8, N 4 each side, and charge 0.

questions.question: Draw the structure of the organic compound Y formed in (b)(i).
questions.answer: Gluconic acid: HOCH2-(CHOH)4-COOH (a carboxylic acid at C1)
steps: Glucose's aldehyde group (CHO) is oxidised to a carboxylic acid (COOH).
Y is therefore CH2OH-CHOH-CHOH-CHOH-CHOH-COOH.

questions.question: Deduce the half-equation for the reaction at the negative electrode of the silver cell, Ag2O + H2O + Zn -> 2Ag + Zn(OH)2.
questions.answer: Zn + 2OH- -> Zn(OH)2 + 2e-
steps: Zinc is oxidised at the negative electrode (0 to +2).
Overall equation minus the positive half-equation gives Zn + 2OH- -> Zn(OH)2 + 2e-.
Check: 2e- lost by Zn match 2e- gained at the positive electrode.

questions.question: Which reagent is most effective at shifting the equilibrium towards chromate(VI) ions? A HCl, B H2SO4, C NaOH, D water.
questions.answer: C - sodium hydroxide
steps: 2CrO4 2- + 2H+ <=> Cr2O7 2- + H2O: chromate forms when H+ is removed.
NaOH is a base and removes H+ from the equilibrium.
So NaOH shifts the equilibrium towards chromate.

questions.question: Which label on the enthalpy profile diagram indicates the intermediate species? (Diagram labels A to D.)
questions.answer: C
steps: An intermediate is a species formed in one step and used in the next, so it sits in a trough (a local minimum) on the enthalpy profile.
On the catalysed pathway the trough between the two peaks is label C.
A is the reactants, and B and D are the peaks (transition states), so the answer is C.

questions.question: What property of iron(III) ions lets them act as homogeneous catalysts for the oxidation of iodide by peroxodisulfate? A they can be oxidised and then reduced, B they can gain and then lose electrons, C they provide a surface, D they form complex intermediates with lower Ea.
questions.answer: A - they can be oxidised and then reduced
steps: Fe3+ is reduced to Fe2+ by I- and then Fe2+ is oxidised back to Fe3+ by S2O8 2-.
This redox cycle is the property that lets Fe3+ act as a catalyst.
Option A describes this most accurately.

questions.question: Which sketch shows the change in concentration of manganate(VII) ions with time in the reaction? (Graph options not in text.)
questions.answer: C: the curve decreases slowly at first, then more steeply, then levels off
steps: The reaction is autocatalysed: the product Mn2+ catalyses it.
At the start there is little Mn2+, so the rate is slow and [MnO4-] falls slowly.
As Mn2+ builds up the rate rises so [MnO4-] falls faster; later the reactants run out, so the curve flattens at zero.
This S-shaped fall is graph C; B is a constant rate, and D is the usual exponential-type fall with no catalytic rise.

questions.question: Which is not a bidentate ligand? A ethanedioate ion, B ethanoate ion, C 1,2-diaminoethane, D 2-aminoethanoic acid.
questions.answer: B - ethanoate ion (monodentate)
steps: Ethanedioate (C2O4 2-) has two O donor pairs and is bidentate.
1,2-diaminoethane has two N donors and is bidentate.
2-aminoethanoic acid (glycinate) has N and O donors and is bidentate.
Ethanoate, CH3COO-, binds through one O atom, so it is not bidentate.

questions.question: Compare and contrast the reactions of aqueous nickel(II) sulfate with NaOH and with ammonia, including what is seen, the equations and the reaction types.
questions.answer: NaOH: green precipitate of [Ni(OH)2(H2O)4], insoluble in excess (acid-base / deprotonation). NH3: the same green precipitate forms (acid-base), then dissolves in excess NH3 to give a blue solution of [Ni(NH3)6]2+ (ligand exchange).
steps: NaOH: a green precipitate forms: [Ni(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH- -> [Ni(OH)2(H2O)4] + 2H2O.
This is an acid-base (deprotonation) reaction giving a precipitate; the green precipitate does not dissolve in excess NaOH.
A little NH3: NH3 acts as a base and the same green precipitate forms: [Ni(H2O)6]2+ + 2NH3 -> [Ni(OH)2(H2O)4] + 2NH4+ (acid-base).
Excess NH3: the precipitate dissolves to give a blue solution: [Ni(OH)2(H2O)4] + 6NH3 -> [Ni(NH3)6]2+ + 2OH- + 4H2O.
Overall this is ligand exchange: [Ni(H2O)6]2+ + 6NH3 -> [Ni(NH3)6]2+ + 6H2O.
Similarity: both reagents first give the green hydroxide precipitate. Difference: only excess NH3 dissolves it, by ligand exchange.

questions.question: Which reaction involves the vanadium oxide catalyst in the contact process, and how does vanadium's oxidation number change? (Options not in text.)
questions.answer: C: SO2 -> SO3 with vanadium changing +5 -> +4 -> +5
steps: V2O5 catalyses the oxidation SO2 + 1/2 O2 -> SO3 in the contact process.
V2O5 (V is +5) oxidises SO2 to SO3 and is itself reduced to V2O4 (V is +4); then O2 oxidises V2O4 back to V2O5 (+5).
So vanadium goes +5 -> +4 -> +5 for the reaction SO2 -> SO3, option C.

questions.question: Which interactions could not occur between CO, NO and the catalytic converter? (Options C and D are blank in the text.)
questions.answer: B: hydrogen bonds
steps: CO, NO, CO2 and N2 contain no H atoms bonded to N, O or F, so they cannot form hydrogen bonds with the converter surface.
The other interactions can occur: covalent bonds in chemisorption to the metal surface, London forces for all molecules, and permanent dipole-induced dipole forces because CO and NO are polar.

questions.question: Name the type of the forward reaction shown in the right-hand electrode systems of the Data Booklet.
questions.answer: Reduction (gain of electrons)
steps: The right-hand electrode systems are written as reduction half-equations (gain of electrons).
So the forward reaction is reduction.

questions.question: Name the series formed when the right-hand electrode systems are placed in order, most negative first.
questions.answer: The electrochemical series
steps: Placing standard electrode potentials in order from most negative to most positive gives the electrochemical series.

questions.question: Identify X and Y in the apparatus used to measure the standard electrode potential for right-hand system 8. (Diagram needed.)
questions.answer: The page shows only the apparatus; X and Y depend on which half-cell is right-hand electrode system 8 in the Data Booklet, and the booklet page is not in the paper.

questions.question: Give two reasons why the initial voltmeter reading may differ from the value in the Data Booklet.
questions.answer: Concentrations are not exactly 1.00 mol dm-3, and the temperature is not exactly 298 K.
steps: Standard electrode potentials need solutions of exactly 1.00 mol dm-3 ion concentration.
Any deviation in concentration changes the electrode potential (Nernst).
The temperature must be 298 K; any other temperature also changes the value.
